opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think right now the place where they're most useful is less about "write me the fastest attention kernel from scratch" and more about being a really good collaborator on the tedious parts of the work.

Kernel writing has a lot of boilerplate. You're managing memory layouts, indexing, figuring out how data moves from global memory to shared memory to registers, handling edge cases when the sequence length isn't a multiple of the block size. A lot of that is pattern-heavy, and models are pretty good at it. If I already know the algorithm I want, say how to tile the computation and where to fuse operations, a model can get me to a working first draft much faster than writing it all by hand.

The part they still struggle with is the hard reasoning about performance. Why is this kernel memory-bound? Is the problem a bank conflict, or register pressure, or poor overlap between compute and data movement? That takes a mental model of the hardware, and it changes with every generation: Hopper versus Blackwell, new tensor core instructions, asynchronous copies. The training data lags the hardware, so models tend to produce code that's correct but leaves a lot of performance on the table.

What I find promising is putting models in a loop with real feedback. You let the model propose a kernel, compile it, run it, check correctness against a reference, profile it, and then feed those numbers back. Kernels are nice because you have a very clear verifier. Either the output matches and it's fast, or it doesn't. That's exactly the setting where search plus a model can do well, a bit like how models get good at math or competitive programming when you can check answers.

There's also a role for higher-level abstractions. Part of what we've tried to do, and what people are doing with Triton and CuTe-style DSLs, is to make the important decisions explicit and the rest automatic. If the language exposes the right knobs, then a model, or a human, only has to reason about the things that actually matter for performance. I think AI and better abstractions reinforce each other there.

So in short: today they're great for accelerating experts and lowering the barrier for people who are new to GPU programming. With tight feedback loops on real hardware, I think we'll see them discover genuinely good kernels, especially for the long tail of operations that no human expert has time to hand-optimize.

r001.rationale: The response says models are most useful as collaborators on tedious kernel-writing work, helping experts produce drafts faster, rather than generating the fastest kernel fully automatically.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, because kernel writing is kind of the thing I've spent a big chunk of my career on. And I'd say the honest answer right now is that the models are most helpful at the parts of the problem that are tedious rather than the parts that are hard.

Let me unpack that a bit. When you write something like FlashAttention, there's really two layers. There's the algorithmic layer, where you're thinking about the memory hierarchy, what lives in SRAM versus HBM, how you tile the computation, how you avoid materializing the attention matrix. That's the insight part, and I don't think the models are generating that for you yet. But then there's this enormous amount of mechanical work below that. Figuring out the right thread block configuration, the pipelining, getting the shared memory layouts right so you don't have bank conflicts, dealing with all the quirks of a specific generation of hardware like Hopper or Blackwell. That stuff is extremely well suited to models, because it's pattern-heavy, it's verifiable, and it's the kind of thing where a human expert knows what good looks like but it still takes days to grind through.

So the first place they're helpful is as a very fast, very knowledgeable pair programmer. You say, I want to pipeline this loop, use the TMA and warp specialization, and it'll give you a draft that's maybe seventy or eighty percent there. That already saves a lot of time, because a lot of the friction in kernel work is just remembering the exact incantation for a given intrinsic.

The second place, and this is the one I'm more excited about, is search. Kernel optimization is fundamentally a search problem over a huge space of implementations, and the nice thing is you have a near-perfect reward signal. The kernel is either correct or it's not, and it's either faster or it's not. You can check both automatically. So you can set up a loop where the model proposes variants, you compile and benchmark them, and feed the results back. That turns the model from a one-shot code generator into something more like an optimizer that happens to have a lot of prior knowledge about GPUs. We've seen this start to work for things like getting a kernel ported to a new architecture, where the structure is known but the tuning is different.

The third thing, which people underrate, is just lowering the barrier. The number of people in the world who can write a high-performance attention or GEMM kernel from scratch is tiny, maybe a few hundred. And the hardware keeps changing, so even those people are constantly relearning. If the models can get a competent ML researcher who's never written CUDA to a reasonably fast kernel, that's a big deal, because it means more ideas actually get tested at the hardware level instead of dying because nobody had time to implement them efficiently.

Where I'd be cautious is on correctness and on the long tail. The models will very confidently produce a kernel that's subtly wrong, numerically off in some edge case, or that works for one shape and falls apart for another. And for the really frontier stuff, like the first implementation on a brand new chip where there's no training data, they're much weaker. So my mental model is: they're great at compressing the time from idea to working baseline, and they're increasingly good at the tuning loop when you give them a real feedback signal. The parts where you need to invent a new way of using the hardware, that's still mostly us, at least for now.

r001.rationale: The response describes models as a fast pair programmer that drafts and tunes kernels, while humans provide the harder algorithmic insights and invent new hardware approaches.

astra-6.text:
I think they're most helpful when you have a really clear feedback loop. You can specify what the operation should do, test whether the generated kernel is correct, and benchmark how fast it runs. Then the model can propose an implementation, see the results, and iterate.

The interesting part is that writing the code is only one piece of the problem. A lot of performance comes from choosing how to break up the computation, how to move data through memory, and what work to assign to each thread. There are lots of possible choices, and the best one can depend on the input shape and the hardware. Models can help explore that space.

So I think of it as automating more of the experimentation. A person can provide the high-level idea, and the model can try different implementations and use measurements to guide the next attempt. Having that feedback is much more useful than just asking it to write a fast kernel in one shot.

r001.rationale: The response describes a person providing the high-level idea while the model explores implementations and iterates using measurements, supporting AI-assisted human collaboration over one-shot automatic generation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re most helpful when you have a really fast feedback loop. You ask the model to write a kernel, check that it’s correct, benchmark it, and then give it the results so it can try again. For kernels, you have a pretty concrete objective: does it produce the right answer, and how fast does it run?

The hard part is often figuring out what to try. Should you change the tile size, use a different memory layout, or fuse two operations? A model can help explore those choices and take care of a lot of the implementation work. But it needs feedback from the actual hardware. Something that looks reasonable in code can perform poorly for reasons you wouldn’t catch just by reading it.

So I’m excited about models as a way to make that experimentation much cheaper. A human can provide the high-level direction, and the model can implement and test a bunch of variations.

r001.rationale: The response says a human can provide high-level direction while the model implements and tests variations, indicating that models may help more when working alongside humans than fully autonomously.
